meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 2: Architecture & Protocol Layers
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: A user clicks 'Allow' on a permission dialog before a tool runs. Which participant is responsible for that decision point?

options.text: The server, which must not execute a tool until the client confirms consent
The client, which sits closest to the server and can block the outgoing request
The model, which decides whether the requested tool is appropriate to call
The host, which enforces security policies and handles user authorization decisions

questions.explanation: The host creates and manages clients, controls connection permissions and lifecycle, enforces security policies and consent requirements, and handles user authorization decisions. Clients route messages; they do not own the consent decision.

questions.question: A tool call returns HTTP 200, but the body contains a JSON-RPC error object. Which layer failed?

options.text: Both: an error body always implies the request never reached the server
Neither: an error inside a 200 is how MCP signals a successful tool failure
The data layer: transport delivery succeeded, MCP semantics did not
The transport layer: a 200 with an error body is a malformed HTTP response

questions.explanation: The transport layer moves and frames bytes; the data layer defines JSON-RPC and MCP semantics. A 200 proves only that the transport worked. Note the contrast with a tool execution failure, which is a normal result carrying isError: true, not an error object.

questions.question: Which statement about server/discover is correct?

options.text: Both sides MUST use it: it replaces initialize as the mandatory first exchange
It is optional on both sides and exists only for the Inspector's UI
Clients MUST call it first; servers MAY implement it if they advertise capabilities
Servers MUST implement it; clients MAY call it before any other request

questions.explanation: Servers MUST implement server/discover. Calling it is optional for clients: a client may invoke any RPC inline and handle UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (-32022) if its version is not supported. It is also the stdio probe for telling modern servers from legacy ones.

questions.question: You move a working server from stdio to Streamable HTTP. Which part of your implementation has to change?

options.text: Only the method names, which carry a different prefix on HTTP transports than on stdio
Neither: the SDK negotiates the transport, so no code changes at all
Only the transport plumbing; the JSON-RPC methods and message shapes are identical
Both: HTTP transports use a REST mapping instead of JSON-RPC messages

questions.explanation: MCP separates a data layer (JSON-RPC 2.0 messages and their semantics) from a transport layer (stdio or Streamable HTTP). The same tools/call looks the same on both; what changes is framing, headers and authorization.

questions.question: How do a client and server learn what each other supports in 2026-07-28?

options.text: Client capabilities ride in every request's _meta; server capabilities come from server/discover
Capabilities are declared in the transport headers and mirrored into the body
The client calls server/discover, and the server calls client/discover in return
Both sides exchange their capabilities once, in the initialize handshake, and cache them for the connection

questions.explanation: There is no handshake. Clients include io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities on every request, and servers advertise theirs in the server/discover result, which clients MAY call but are not required to.

questions.question: In one host, the CRM server's calls fail while the filesystem server's calls succeed. What does the architecture tell you about where to look?

options.text: At that one client-server relationship: its config, transport, authorization or server
At the host's client pool, since a single client multiplexes both of the server connections
At the shared session store, because both servers read the same session state
At the model, since it selects which server's tools to call for each request

questions.explanation: Each client talks to exactly one server, so a failure confined to one server lives in that relationship. A host-wide fault would affect both. There is no shared session store: 2026-07-28 removed protocol sessions.

questions.question: A gateway process exposes tools to a host and, to answer them, calls three upstream MCP servers itself. Is that allowed, and what is it?

options.text: Yes, but only if the gateway declares itself a proxy in server/discover
Yes: one process can be a server to its caller and a client to its upstreams
No: a process must pick one role, so the gateway must proxy raw bytes instead
No: chaining is possible only through the registry, which brokers the connections

questions.explanation: Roles are per-connection, not per-process, so composition is normal: the gateway is a server downstream and a client upstream. It carries the usual server duties toward its caller, including not passing tokens through to upstreams.
